newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU unlikely to restore wheat export subsidy soon.
newsitem.headline: EU unlikely to restore wheat export subsidy soon.

text.p: PARIS, Sept 5 (Reuter) The European Union is unlikely to restore export subsidies for wheat as long as some exporters are ready to pay an export tax, officials close to the EU executive said on Thursday.
"Why would Brussels grant refunds when there are demands for taxes?," said one official familiar with EU thinking.
The EU has been facing pressure to relax its tight grip on wheat exports ahead of a promising grain harvest.
Last year the European Union imposed an export tax on wheat to curb exports in view of low stocks and rising prices at home.

On Thursday, traders bidding in France asked to export 72,350 tonnes of soft wheat with taxes ranging from 0.02 to 0.75 Ecus per tonne and 97,500 tonnes of soft wheat at refunds from 1.00 to 8.57 Ecus per tonne at this week's EU grain tender.
Last week the EU agreed to pay an export subsidy of 3.9 Ecus per tonne to help the sale of wheat to African, Caribbean and Pacific nations, who depend on EU for trade relef.

But it refused all bids to export free-market wheat with subsidies in its main tender and awarded the export of 147,500 tonnes of soft wheat at a tax of 0.50 Ecus per tonne, making it worth some $185 per tonne, FOB.
"If some countries are willing to pay $185 per tonne, FOB, for European wheat, Brussels is not interested in selling it for less," the official said.

Several traders said they were convinced the EU may wait a few more weeks before restoring wheat subsidies. They said the Commission may want to see how the harvest and the export scene shape up before before making a move.
"The Commission will eventually come up with a refund but it may want to wait a while," one trade source said.

Traders estimate operators may bid for taxes throughout September to cover mostly a few deals with eastern Europe. Once these deals are covered, some traders said Brussels may consider whether to award subsidies to help sales clinched at world market prices. --Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432
